etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English wowen, woȝen, from Old English wōgian (“to woo, court, marry”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Scots wow (“to woo”). Perhaps related to Old English wōg, wōh (“bending, crookedness”), in the specific sense of "bend or incline (some)one toward oneself". If so, then derived from Proto-Germanic *wanhō (“a bend, angle”), from Proto-Indo-European *wonk- (“crooked, bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *wā- (“to bend, twist, turn”); related to Old Norse vá (“corner, angle”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To endeavor to gain someone's affection/support.
(transitive, often of a man) To try to persuade (someone) to be in an amorous relationship with

quote.citation: 1485, Thomas Malory, Le Morte Darthur Book XIX, Chapter viii, leaf 393v:
quote.text: Soo leue we syr Launcelot lyenge within that caue in grete payne / and euery day ther came a lady & brouȝt hym his mete & his drynke / & wowed hym to haue layne by hym / and euer the noble knyghte syre Launcelot sayd her nay."So leave we Sir Launcelot lying within that cave in great pain; and every day there came a lady and brought him his meat and his drink, and wooed him, to have lain by him; and ever the noble knight, Sir Launcelot, said her nay."

quote.citation: 1594, [William Shakespeare], Venus and Adonis, 2nd edition, London:  […]  Richard Field, […], →OCLC, [verse 17], lines [97–100]:
quote.text: I haue beene wooed, as I intreat thee now, / Euen by the ſterne, and direfull God of warre, / VVhoſe ſinowie necke in battel nere did bow, / VVho conquers where he comes in euery iarre;  […]

quote.citation: 1718, Matthew Prior, epistle to Charles Montagu.:
quote.text: Each, like the Grecian artist, wooes  / The image he himself has wrought.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To court solicitously; to invite with importunity; to solicit in love.

quote.citation: a. 1645, John Milton, “Il Penseroso”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC, page 39:
quote.text: Thee Chauntreſs oft the Woods among, / I woo to hear thy eeven Song;

quote.citation: a. 1850, William Cullen Bryant, Summer Wind:
quote.text: I woo the wind / That still delays his coming.

quote.citation: 1962 April, “Death from Natural Causes?”, in Modern Railways, page 218:
quote.text: It will be a tragedy if further enterprises of this kind—for example, the one proposed between South Wales, Bristol and the South Coast via Salisbury—are now deferred until they, too, are realised too late to make an impact on a public that is too firmly wedded to the roads to be wooed back to the trains.

definitions.definition: (slang) Expressing joy or excitement; woohoo, yahoo.
